cards.back:
**A SOCKS**
**A** — **Assessment** *(uncovering and prioritizing risks)*
**S** — **Sponsorship** *(gaining & demonstrating leadership support)*
**O** — **Organizational optimization** *(aligning jobs and processes with the new environment)*
**C** — **Communications** *(designing and delivering key messages)*
**K** — **Knowledge transfer** *(capturing and sharing lessons learned)*
**S** — **Skills development** *(org change management training)*

*Communications **spans the other five** but has its own focus as well.*

cards.front: **Hammer's definition of reengineering** + the three concepts
cards.back:
> *"A **fundamental rethinking** and **radical redesign** of business processes to achieve **dramatic improvements** in critical, contemporary measures of performance — such as **cost, quality, service, and speed**."*

**Mnemonic: BPR is FRD**
**F**undamental rethinking → how you *think*
**R**adical redesign → what you *design*
**D**ramatic improvements → what you *achieve*

**"Select The Doctor, Redesign, Prototype, Implement"**
1. **S**election of process to be redesigned
2. **T**eam — have the reengineering team in place
3. **D**iagnosis — process diagnosis
4. **R**edesign — process redesign
5. **P**rototyping
6. **I**mplementation — full scale

*Diagnosis **before** redesign is non-negotiable — prescribing before diagnosing is failure reason 5.*

**SPAS**
**S**cenario (L1) → **P**rocess (L2) → **A**ctivity (L3) → **S**tep (L4)

**Worked example:**
Supply Chain Management → Order Management → Delivery Scheduling → Calculation of Delivery Date

*Needed because a medium-sized company has **40–100 processes**.*

$$\textbf{Plan} \cdot \textbf{Source} \cdot \textbf{Make} \cdot \textbf{Deliver} \cdot \textbf{Return}$$

**Source → Make → Deliver** is the physical flow; **Return** is the reverse flow; **Plan** sits *above* all four.

Spans **Suppliers' Supplier → Supplier → Your Company → Customer → Customer's Customer**, with the four operational processes **repeating at every link**.

cards.front: **AS-IS vs TO-BE modelling** — how much detail?
cards.back:
**AS-IS shallow, TO-BE deep.**

**AS-IS** — *"no need of much detailed analysis as anyway the process will not be used in future."* High level only: **why the process exists · what it does · its high-level objective**.

**TO-BE** — *"needs to be detailed so that every step is clear to users"*: **all input–output relationships, data flows, organization roles**.

*Getting this backwards is BPR failure reason 1 — **As-Is analysis paralysis**.*

**Analysis · People · Execution (A-P-E)**

**Analysis:** too much AS-IS analysis (paralysis) · poor scoping
**People:** ignore people concerns · not putting best people in project · no top management support
**Execution:** little change — not redesign · copying another BPR design blindly · large scale implementation without prototyping

*The **people** family is the largest.*

| Parameter | TQM | BPR |
|---|---|---|
| Level of change | **Incremental** | **Radical** |
| Starting point | **Existing process** | **Clean slate** |
| Frequency | **Continuous** | **One-time** |
| Time required | Short term | Long term |
| Participation | **Bottom up** | **Top down** |
| Typical scope | Narrow | Broad |
| Risk | Moderate | **High** |
| Primary enabler | **Statistical control** | **IT** |
| Type of change | Cultural | **Cultural / Structural** |

*Graph: TQM is a **slope**, BPR is a **step**. Every row follows from that shape.*

**Three fears — Job, System, Payoff (J-S-P):**

**Fear for the job** — *What will be my new role? Will my job remain? Do I go back to my old place?*
**Fear of the system** — *Will I be able to operate it? Can I cope with new technology?*
**Doubt about the payoff** — ***What's in it for me?*** *Will my new skill be valued later?*

*Lead with **WIIFM** — and note the resistance is **rational**: the org gets the benefits, the individual gets more work.*

**Level 1 — Handle fear and uncertainty** *(key: **communication**)*
**Communicate · Training · Power users and ERP champions · Round-the-clock help desk · Leadership support**

**Level 2 — Getting motivated and committed** *(key: **organizational design**)*
**Involve employees in decisions · design incentive schemes and performance measures · design new and more interesting roles**

*You cannot skip to Level 2 — **a frightened employee cannot be motivated**.*

**Four kinds of waste:**
**Logistics** — **Storing** items · **Moving** material
**Control** — **Checks & controls** · **Inspection**
**Failure** — **Reworking** · **Reconciliation**
**Urgency** — **Expediting**

*Caution: NVA ≠ useless. Some have value such as **management information** — **retain or transfer** that into another step rather than deleting.*

**Case Manager is a Single Point Of Contact (SPOC) for a process.**

**Before:** Credit request → Financing → Credit checking → Approval → Issuance → Credit decision
**After:** Credit request → **Case manager** → Credit decision

Four departments become one role — **three hand-offs, their queues and their reconciliations all vanish.**

*Only possible because **IT** gives one person the information four departments used to hold.*

$$\textbf{BE} = \textbf{BPR} + \textbf{IT}$$

**IT changes the rules of business — disruptive:**
- Data available **anywhere to anybody** with control
- Software enables **even a non-expert to do an expert job**
- **Decision support tools for everybody**
- **Plans get revised instantaneously**

*Caveat: **"BPR is possible without IT also!"** — the equation is a scoping statement for this course.*

**Risks of full-blown BPR before ERP:**
- takes long time and cost
- **no guarantee the best-designed processes will be supported by the ERP**
- may take 3–4 years, by which time business dynamics change

**The middle path:** follow the **best practice processes that come with the ERP**, and do a **limited BPR** where it gives **competitive advantage**.

**Rule: standardise where you don't compete; differentiate where you do.**

*Proverb: **"Old process + new technology = costly old process."***

From **186 ERP implementations** surveyed by the **Gartner Group**:
- **< 25% deliver hard monetary benefits**
- **70% of failed projects did not use performance metrics**
- **27% did not measure** at all

*Organizational change is difficult because of **"human" elements**, mostly — the deck's name for it is **"Human Inertia."***

**Core Change Team** — **implements** organizational change management steps; reports to **Project Sponsor and Manager**; **dedicated** resources from **HR, OD professionals and/or consulting**; ideally a **mix of long and short-term employees**.

**Extended Change Team** — **introduces and conducts risk assessments, communicates, implements action plans**; **part-time** members from **line management or consulting**.

**Change Team Lead** — must **know the organization well and be well-respected**; becomes the **symbolic face** of the programme.

*Both teams are generally **not part of the primary implementation team**.*

**2 leaders, 2 doers, 2 coordinators:**

**Leaders** — **Leader** *(= the Project Manager; identifies key processes, appoints process owners, establishes measures and rewards)* · **Steering Committee** *(settles inter-process disputes, priority, resources)*

**Doers** — **Process Owner** *(SME; appoints the team, **supports and protects radically new ideas**, manages the process afterwards)* · **Reengineering Team** *(redesigns, **sells the design to the people**, continues to implementation)*

**Coordinators** — **Reengineering Coordinator** *(the "hard" part)* · **Change Coordinator** *(**"conscience keeper of the leader"**)*

> *"A process model is a **visual representation** of different activities and steps of the process, **data flows** of inputs and outputs for different steps of the process."*

It can also show **which organizational entity runs the process**. It is a **design representation** of a business process.

**Also known as:** Process Modelling · Process Mapping

*Key benefit: **bridges the gap between IT people and business users who generally do not speak the same language.***

**EPC** (Event Driven Process Chains) → **IDS Scheer** → **ARIS** framework → originally to illustrate **SAP** processes

**BPMN** (Business Process Model and Notation) → developed by **BPMI**, maintained by **OMG** since the **2005** merger → maps to **BPEL** (Business Process Execution Language)

**UML** → **Rational Software** (three OO methodologists) → **Rational Unified Process**; for **software object modelling**, not business processes

cards.front: **The five dimensions of a process model**
cards.back:
**G-R-I-O-A**, in maturity order:
**G**raphical — the pictorial representation
**R**esource — define all resources so they can be associated
**I**nformation — a view of data and how it is used
**O**rganization — definition and structure of organization units
**A**nalysis — key process metrics and attributes defined and analyzed

*Graphics (what happens) → Resources (what it needs) → Information (what data flows) → Organization (who does it) → Analysis (how well it performs).*

**BPM models one process**; **BM models the whole enterprise as one large system.**

**BM definition:** *"a visual representation of an enterprise's business as **one large system** showing different **subsystems**, what processes they support, the **interconnection** between them, and how **data flows** between them."*

**BM's distinctive contribution:** it shows the **future application landscape** — *which processes ERP takes, **where legacy applications will remain**, and how data flows between them.*

**Set up → Communicate → Sustain → Close**

**Project Preparation** — change management plan · identify **change sponsors for all locations** · assign core team roles · create extended team
**Business Blueprinting** — **change communication framework** · conduct change management training
**Realization** — **sustain** sponsorship & communications · team building · knowledge transfer
**Go Live & Closing** — resolve open issues · **address impact of withdrawal of legacy systems** · lessons learned · **disband and recognize**

*Answer to "when?" — **all throughout**.*

1. **Roles and responsibilities** — change or new emerge
2. **Measurements and incentives** — **at process level rather than individual functional**
3. **Information Technology**
4. **Organizational structure** — **flattened hierarchy**
5. **Skills** — **multi-skilling**

*They are **interdependent**, so you switch over in stages: "set the levers in 1-2-2 state, stabilize, shift to 3-4-4, stabilize…"*

1. **Leadership and top management commitment**
2. **Prototype every process** before large scale implementation
3. **Show early success within the first three to six months**
4. **Results to be measurable**
5. **Communicate effectively to manage change**
6. **Proper change management**

*Four of the six map directly onto a named **reason for failure** — the two lists are the same content read from opposite ends.*

*Deck's note: **"Leadership must believe in the new system."***

> *"The process of **comparing one's business processes and performance metrics to industry bests** and/or best practices from other industries."*

**Five types:** **Process · Financial · Competitiveness · Product · Functional**

**Steps:** identify focus area → identify leaders/competition/standards → identify measures/best practices → align & implement

**Exemplars:** **Toyota — JIT** · **Motorola — Six Sigma** · **Wal-Mart — VMI**

*Pitfall: **"comparing apples to oranges."***

cards.front: **Common process problems** and why they exist
cards.back:
**Problems:** no **end-to-end ownership** · **too many hand-offs** · **wrong measurements (task rather than process performance)** · **sequential execution** · many audits/reconciliations that add no customer value · very few steps are value-adding

**Why they arose:**
1. **Non-availability of technology in the beginning**
2. **Process copied from another company / parent org**
3. **Brought in as a temporary measure, never reviewed**
4. **Process there to suit some set of individuals**

*"Many of these are problems **because one is looking at it**. Else they continue to be the way of working!"*

> *"A business process is a **set of logically related tasks** that use the **resources of an organization** to achieve a **defined business outcome**."*

- Has a **clear beginning and end**, and **clearly identified inputs and outputs**
- Is **cross-functional**, not restricted within a single function

**Four principles:** it has a number of **steps** · each step has **specific input and output** · each step can be run by a **separate organizational entity** · **each step should add value** to the whole process

**Objective (learn verbatim):**
> *"**The architecture of the organization needs to be aligned with the new process and technology.**"*

**Means:** new/defined **roles and responsibilities** · new/defined **reporting structure** · **job descriptions** · new/defined **performance measures and incentive systems**

**The cascade:**
$$\textbf{New technology} \rightarrow \textbf{new processes} \rightarrow \textbf{new roles} \rightarrow \textbf{new structure} \rightarrow \textbf{new measures \& incentives}$$

*The last step is the one organisations stop short of.*
